title: HVAC Tips for Dry Southern California Weather
h1: How Do I Keep My Home Comfortable With HVAC in a Dry Climate?
description: Dry inland heat and Santa Ana winds are hard on homes and HVAC systems. These tips cover humidity, filters, dust, cooling efficiency and when to get help.
quick_answer: In dry weather, keep indoor humidity in a comfortable range with a humidifier if needed, change filters more often because dust builds up faster, keep the outdoor unit clean, seal ducts and the home to keep dust and heat out, and use your thermostat wisely. Regular tune-ups help your system handle hot, dry stretches.
body:
How does dry weather affect my home and HVAC system?

Much of San Diego County and Orange County is dry for a good part of the year, especially inland. When Santa Ana winds blow in from the desert, humidity can drop sharply and temperatures climb, even near the coast. That dry air pulls moisture from skin, sinuses, wood floors and furniture.

Dry conditions also mean more dust and, during fire season, smoke. Your HVAC system has to filter more particles and work harder during hot stretches, so a little extra care pays off.

Should I use a humidifier?

If you notice dry skin, cracked lips, static shocks, nosebleeds or a scratchy throat, indoor air may be too dry. A comfortable indoor humidity range for most homes is roughly 30 to 50 percent. A simple humidity monitor shows where you are.

  • Portable humidifiers work well for a bedroom. Clean them often to prevent mold and bacteria.
  • Whole-home humidifiers connect to the HVAC system and add moisture to the air throughout the house.

Don't overdo it. Too much humidity can cause condensation and mold. In coastal homes, humidity is usually high enough most of the year, so humidifiers are more often useful inland or during Santa Ana events.

Dry weather can also be hard on wood floors, cabinets and furniture, which may shrink, gap or crack. If you've noticed that alongside dry-air symptoms, a whole-home humidifier is worth discussing, since it protects the house as well as the people in it.

Why do I need to change filters more often?

Dry, windy weather kicks up dust and pollen, and wildfire smoke adds fine particles. All of it ends up in your filter faster. A clogged filter reduces airflow, makes the system work harder and can lead to a frozen coil or overheating.

Dust also settles on the outdoor coil and blower wheel. A dirty blower wheel moves less air even with a clean filter, so it's worth having it checked during a tune-up if your home sees a lot of dust.

Check your filter monthly during dry, windy months and fire season. A good pleated filter or a whole-home media air cleaner can make a big difference in dust and smoke.

How do I keep dust and heat out?

  1. Close windows and doors on Santa Ana days and during smoke events.
  2. Seal gaps around doors, windows and the attic hatch with weatherstripping and caulk.
  3. Seal and insulate ducts in the attic, where leaks pull in hot, dusty air.
  4. Add attic insulation to keep summer heat from pouring down into living space.
  5. Use shades or blinds on sun-facing windows in the afternoon.

Our duct sealing and repair service tackles the leaks that let dust and heat into the system.

How can I keep cooling efficient in hot, dry weather?

  • Keep the outdoor unit clean. Dust and leaves on the coil reduce its ability to release heat. Rinse it gently with a hose, never a pressure washer, and keep plants trimmed back.
  • Set the thermostat sensibly. Raising it a few degrees while you're away and lowering it before you return saves energy without overworking the system.
  • Use ceiling fans to feel cooler at a higher thermostat setting. Turn them off when you leave the room, since fans cool people, not rooms.
  • Run heat-producing appliances like the oven and dryer in the cooler parts of the day, such as early morning or after sunset.
  • Schedule a spring tune-up before the first hot inland stretch so the AC is ready.

When should I call a technician?

Call for service if the system struggles to keep up on a normal hot day, blows warm air, short cycles, or makes unusual noises. Dry, hot weather puts the most stress on an AC, so small issues tend to show up then. Our HVAC technicians can tune up your system, check refrigerant and airflow, and recommend humidifiers or filtration that fit your home.
faqs: What humidity level should I keep my house at?
Roughly 30 to 50 percent is comfortable for most people and homes. Below that, skin and sinuses dry out and wood can crack. Above it, mold and dust mites become more likely.
Does air conditioning dry out the air?
Yes. AC removes moisture as it cools, which helps in humid weather but can make already dry air feel drier. A humidifier can help if you notice dry-air symptoms.
How do Santa Ana winds affect my HVAC system?
They bring hot, dry, dusty air and sometimes wildfire smoke. Filters clog faster, the AC works harder, and dust can get into leaky ducts. Keep windows closed and check your filter often.
Is an evaporative cooler a good option in dry climates?
Evaporative coolers work best in hot, very dry areas. Near the coast, where humidity is higher, they are much less effective. Most homes here are better served by central AC or a heat pump.
